title: U.S. Navy Commissions Flight III Destroyer USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128) in Alaska
summary: The U.S. Navy has officially commissioned the USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), its newest Flight III Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer, in Whittier, Alaska. This advanced vessel is equipped with the SPY-6 radar and Aegis Baseline 10 combat system, representing the latest iteration of the Burke-class destroyers.
detail:
The U.S. Navy has commissioned the USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), its newest Flight III Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer, marking its official entry into active service. This event is significant because the USS Ted Stevens represents a major leap in naval capability, primarily due to its integration of the advanced SPY-6 radar and Aegis Baseline 10 combat system.

The Arleigh Burke-class destroyers are the backbone of the U.S. Navy's surface fleet, known for their multi-mission capabilities, including anti-air, anti-surface, and anti-submarine warfare. The "Flight III" designation signifies the latest and most capable variant, specifically designed to accommodate the powerful SPY-6 (AN/SPY-6(V)1) Air and Missile Defense Radar. This new radar provides vastly improved detection and tracking capabilities for ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and aircraft simultaneously, significantly enhancing the ship's ability to defend against complex threats.

The Aegis Baseline 10 combat system is the software and hardware suite that integrates the SPY-6 radar, allowing the ship to process and act on the advanced data it collects. This upgrade is crucial for maintaining the U.S. Navy's technological edge and its capacity for ballistic missile defense (BMD) in an evolving global threat landscape. Commissioning such an advanced warship reinforces the Navy's ability to project power, ensure maritime security, and protect national interests worldwide. The ship is named after Senator Ted Stevens, a distinguished Alaskan politician and World War II veteran.

title: Mind-reading tech aims to make AI actually intelligent
summary: Scientists, including those at KAIST, have developed a system that can detect unspoken "That's not what I meant" responses directly from human brainwaves using EEG. This brain-computer interface aims to allow AI to understand user intent more accurately and correct misunderstandings in real-time, moving towards more genuinely intelligent interactions.

title: Smart wallpaper turns your wall into a small indoor powerplant
summary: Researchers at Binghamton University have developed a new technology that can generate a small electric current from indoor humidity. Described in Advanced Energy Materials, this "smart wallpaper" concept explores the potential for electricity generation from within homes, complementing traditional rooftop solar.

title: Boeing wins 'mystery fighter' contract for US Navy
summary: Boeing has secured a US$20-billion contract from the US Navy to develop the F/A-XX 6th-Generation fighter plane. Details about this "super-secret" aircraft remain largely undisclosed, with only glimpses of its design having been seen.

title: Dairy waste could be a sweet new source of biofuel
summary: Researchers, including those from Heriot Watt University, are exploring salty whey, a byproduct of cheese manufacturing, as a new source for biofuel. This innovative approach aims to convert dairy waste into energy, offering a sustainable solution for both waste management and fuel production.

title: V2G system sucks energy out of parked EVs to supply the grid
summary: A Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) system is being developed that allows parked electric vehicles (EVs) to supply electricity back to the grid. This innovation aims to turn EVs from mere consumers into active participants in grid stability, addressing the challenge of increased electricity demand from EV adoption.
